title: False sharing: cache line invalidation, padding, @Contended
keyPoints: False sharing occurs when two threads write to different variables that reside on the same CPU cache line (typically 64 bytes), causing constant cache invalidation between cores.
Each write invalidates the entire cache line on other cores, even though the other thread's variable was not modified.
Performance degrades 10-100x for what looks like completely independent, non-shared data.
Fix with manual padding: insert 7 long fields (56 bytes) between the two hot variables to separate them onto different cache lines.
Fix with @jdk.internal.vm.annotation.Contended (Java 8+): the JVM automatically inserts 128 bytes of padding around the annotated field.
LongAdder is fast because its internal Cell class uses @Contended to place each cell on its own cache line, eliminating false sharing.
False sharing is invisible in standard profilers and lock contention tools; it can only be detected with hardware cache miss counters (perf stat, JMH @AuxCounters).

s1_definition.oneliner: False sharing is a performance problem where two threads writing to independent variables on the same CPU cache line cause constant cross-core cache invalidation, degrading throughput by 10-100x even though no data is actually shared.
s1_definition.profdef:
- **Cache line** – the smallest unit of data transfer between CPU cache and main memory, typically 64 bytes on modern CPUs.
- **False sharing** – two variables fit on the same 64-byte cache line. Thread-1 writes variable-A on Core-1. The CPU invalidates the entire cache line on Core-2, even though Thread-2 only uses variable-B (which was not modified). Thread-2 must reload the line from L3 cache or main memory. This ping-pong happens on every write.
- **Manual padding** – insert dummy fields (7 longs = 56 bytes) between hot variables to push them onto separate cache lines.
- **@Contended** – `@jdk.internal.vm.annotation.Contended` tells the JVM to insert padding automatically (128 bytes by default). Requires `-XX:-RestrictContended` or internal module access.
- **LongAdder** – uses `@Contended` on its internal `Cell` class so each thread's cell occupies its own cache line, which is why LongAdder is 10x faster than AtomicLong under high contention.
s1_definition.analogy: Two tellers at National Bank of India sit at separate desks with their own calculators, but the calculators are placed on the same small shared shelf. When Rajesh presses a button on his calculator, the entire shelf vibrates, resetting Priya's calculator display. Priya must re-read her number. They are not sharing data, they are sharing the shelf (cache line). The fix is to give each teller their own shelf (padding). No more vibration, no more interference.

sections.s3_flow:
```text
  False Sharing: Two Variables, One Cache Line
  ════════════════════════════════════════════

  Without padding (false sharing):
  ┌──────────────────── Cache Line (64 bytes) ────────────────────┐
  │ [object header 16B] [buyCounter 8B] [sellCounter 8B] [pad]   │
  └──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────-┘
  Core-1 writes buyCounter → INVALIDATES entire line on Core-2
  Core-2 writes sellCounter → INVALIDATES entire line on Core-1
  Constant ping-pong! 10-100x slower!

  With padding (no false sharing):
  ┌──────────── Cache Line 1 (64 bytes) ─────────────┐
  │ [object header 16B] [buyCounter 8B] [padding 40B] │
  └───────────────────────────────────────────────────┘
  ┌──────────── Cache Line 2 (64 bytes) ─────────────┐
  │ [sellCounter 8B] [padding 56B]                    │
  └───────────────────────────────────────────────────┘
  Core-1 writes buyCounter → Line 2 NOT affected
  Core-2 writes sellCounter → Line 1 NOT affected
  Independent! Full speed!
```
sections.s6_takeaway:
False sharing is a hardware-level performance trap where two threads writing to independent variables on the same 64-byte cache line cause constant cross-core cache invalidation. Each write forces the other core to reload the entire line, turning a 1-5 nanosecond L1 cache hit into a 40-100 nanosecond L3 or main memory access. The result is 10-100x slower throughput for operations that appear completely independent in the source code.

The fix is padding: insert enough dummy bytes between hot variables to ensure each one occupies its own cache line. Manual padding uses 7 long fields (56 bytes) between variables. The @Contended annotation tells the JVM to insert 128 bytes of padding automatically. LongAdder is fast because its internal Cell class uses @Contended, placing each thread's counter on its own cache line.

False sharing is invisible in standard profilers because there is no lock contention to measure. It can only be detected with hardware cache miss counters. At a high-frequency trading desk at National Bank of India, buy and sell counters on adjacent fields ran at 50 million operations per second. After padding, throughput jumped to 480 million, a nearly 10x improvement.

Remember one sentence: false sharing happens when independent variables share a cache line, and the fix is padding them apart so each variable has its own 64-byte line.
